title: The long view in construction
excerpt: Civic building is measured in decades, not quarters. A note on why the group still specifies for the second generation of a structure's users rather than the first.
body: There is a question that gets asked on every civic project, usually late and usually by someone under pressure: does this need to be this good? The honest answer is that nobody involved in the conversation will be there when it matters. The building will outlast the contract, the team and in most cases the organisation that commissioned it.

That is the argument for specifying to the second generation of a structure's users rather than the first. The first generation inherits a building in its best condition and forgives a great deal. The second inherits whatever the first generation's maintenance budget allowed, and it is their experience that reveals whether the original decisions were sound.

In practice this shows up in unglamorous choices. Materials that can be repaired with ordinary skill and ordinary parts. Services routed so they can be reached without opening a finished surface. Details drawn so that the obvious way to maintain them is also the correct way, because the obvious way is what will actually happen.

None of it photographs well. A building that has been specified this way looks, on handover day, much like one that has not. The difference emerges slowly and is only ever visible to people who were not in the room.
